stops.name: The hermitage, the hind of God
stops.campa: A hind comes out of the forest to the hermit: a fair doe, sent and provisioned by God for exactly this office. At certain hours she comes to the cave and gives the old man her milk, and this is his whole table. The gentle economy runs for seasons: the man prays, the deer arrives punctual as a bell, the forest witnesses. She is not tamed and he is not fed by men; both live directly out of the hand of God, who keeps a creature for every hermit and an hour for every mercy.
stops.quote: A fair hind, which without doubt was purveyed of God for to nourish him, and at certain hours ministered her milk to him.

stops.name: The thicket, the royal hunt and the hounds that halt
stops.campa: The king's hunt enters the forest: Flavius Wamba, king of the Goths, with hounds and horns and knights. The pack sights the fair hind and runs her hard through the trees; she flies to the feet of the man she nourishes. And at the thicket the hounds stop. They cannot come on; they circle and bay at a hedge of thorn as at a wall of iron, and no huntsman can force them a step nearer. The horns call confusion. Something is in that thicket that dogs may not touch, and the king wants to know what.

stops.name: The thicket, the arrow through the hermit's hand
stops.campa: Next day the hunt returns and rings the thicket. The hind breaks for the cave; a knight, to start her, looses an arrow blind into the thorn. Giles has thrown up his hand to shield the fleeing doe, and the shaft passes through the hand that shields her. The hunters hack a way in and find an old man white-haired at prayer, the hind pressed against him, the arrow in his flesh, and not one word of complaint. Blood on the milk-giver's guardian: in this instant the patron of cripples is made, wounded for a creature, crowned by a wound.
stops.quote: One of the knights drew up an arrow follily for to make it afeard and spring out, but he wounded and hurt the holy man, which ceased not to pray for the fair hind.

stops.name: The cave, the wound refused healing; the king's awe
stops.campa: King and bishop come humbly now, on foot, to the pierced hermit. They send physicians; he sends them away. He prays instead that the wound never close in this life, keeping the arrow's work as his mortification, for he knows that virtue is made perfect in infirmity. The king returns and returns, drawn as the hounds were held back, and lays treasures at the cave mouth; Giles refuses every coin, then relents only this far: let the gold build a house for monks. The king seizes the answer like a grant of grace.
stops.quote: He prayed our Lord that he might never be whole thereof in his life, for he knew well that virtue should profit to him in infirmity.

stops.name: Saint-Gilles-du-Gard, the abbey rises over the cave
stops.campa: On the king's gold and the hermit's ground, a monastery rises in the Vallée Flavienne: the church set directly over the cave, so that the altar stands above the bed of stone where the hind gave milk. Masons where the hounds bayed; a cloister where the thicket stood. Giles watches the walls go up around his solitude and understands the bargain God has struck with him: the world he fled will now be organized, in ranks and habits, around the very hole he hid in. The place will bear his name when the king's is dust.

stops.name: Saint-Gilles-du-Gard, the abbot's staff taken
stops.campa: Long he refuses the office: the man who would not keep a coat will not gladly keep a community. But the king presses and the brothers kneel, and at last Giles takes the abbot's staff in the hand the arrow made holy. The wound governs well: no discipline in the house is harsher than the one the abbot keeps on himself, and none gentler than the one he keeps on others. Monks gather to the rule; the poor gather to the gate; the hind's economy, scaled up, becomes a great house of mercy by the Rhône.

stops.name: Rome, the Pope's blessing and the cypress doors
stops.campa: The abbot goes to Rome to set his house under Peter. The Pope receives him, grants the abbey its privileges, and gives him a gift of weight: two great doors of cypress, carved with the images of the apostles Peter and Paul. Doors: for the man whose life has been a series of doors closed against fame and opened by God. But cypress doors do not ride pack-mules across the Alps. Giles looks at the gift, and then at the Tiber running yellow past the city, and trusts the carrier that has never failed him.

stops.name: The Tiber, the doors cast on the water
stops.campa: At the river's edge Giles has the cypress doors carried down and thrown into the Tiber, commending them to God for pilot, freight-master and crew. The doors do not sink. They take the current like swans, Peter and Paul face-up to heaven, and go down the river toward Ostia and the open sea while the abbot turns north by land, unburdened. Rome has seen triumphs on that water, but never cargo shipped with pure prayer for a bill of lading. The doors are sailing themselves to Provence.
stops.quote: He threw them into the Tiber at Rome, and recommended them to God for to govern.

stops.name: The gate of the abbey, the doors arrive before the abbot
stops.campa: Down the Tiber, across the whole width of the sea, into the Rhône's mouth and up the channel to the abbey landing: when Giles comes home over the mountains, the cypress doors are waiting for him at the monastery gate, dry-faced, punctual, having beaten him to Provence. The brothers hang them where they docked themselves. Peter and Paul now stand door-keepers to the hermit's cave, and every pilgrim who will ever push through them enters on a miracle before setting foot on the floor.

stops.name: Orléans, the Mass of Saint Giles: the angel and the scroll
stops.campa: The king of the Franks summons the abbot north: Charles, whom the tradition names Charlemagne, for here the vita folds time a second time, holding Goth-king and emperor in one hermit's lifetime, and the fold is true. Charles carries a sin so foul he dare not speak it in any confession. Giles says the Mass for him, and as he prays, the angel of the Lord descends and lays a scroll on the altar with the unspoken sin written out entire, and as the hermit prays on, the writing fades letter by letter until the page is clean. The unconfessable is forgiven; the king weeps like a boy.
stops.quote: The angel of our Lord appeared to him, and laid a schedule upon the altar where the sin of the king was written.

stops.name: Nîmes, the prince's son raised
stops.campa: Homeward from the king's court, Giles passes through Nîmes on the day the prince's son is carried out dead, the house loud with mourning. The abbot goes in to the body as calmly as to a sleeping guest, prays, and gives the boy back to his father alive: the vita's resurrection, done in a doorway, almost in passing. The man who refused to have his own hand healed spends the great cures freely on others. Nîmes never forgets; the city keeps the story like a relic.

stops.name: Saint-Gilles-du-Gard, the death of the abbot, 1 September
stops.campa: The abbot announces his death beforehand, as a man names the hour of a ship's sailing, and exhorts the brothers to charity. On the first of September he sleeps and dies goodly in the Lord, above the cave, behind the doors that sailed themselves, the arrow-wound still open in his hand as he had prayed it would be. Many bear witness that they hear the company of angels bearing his soul to heaven: the last fame of the man who fled fame, and this one he cannot escape either. The Church keeps the day forever.
stops.quote: So he slept and died goodly in our Lord. And many witness that they heard the company of angels bearing the soul of him into heaven.
